title: Disease and Development: The Effect of Life Expectancy on Economic Growth
research_question: What is the effect of increases in population health and longevity on aggregate economic activity, including population size, total output, and output per capita? Do exogenous improvements in health conditions translate into faster growth in income per person, or are the gains absorbed primarily by larger populations?
data_description: The authors assemble a country-level panel covering 59 countries (a base sample from Western Europe, the Americas, Oceania, and Asia) with decadal observations from 1940 to 1980, plus pre-period data back to 1900/1930 for falsification and extensions through 2000 and to sub-Saharan Africa for robustness. Key variables include life expectancy at birth, total population, total births, infant mortality, GDP, GDP per capita, GDP per working-age population, years of schooling, and investment rates. Demographic data come from UN Demographic Yearbooks and League of Nations reports; GDP and population from Maddison (2003); schooling from Barro-Lee. The authors also hand-collect country-level mortality rates around 1940 for 15 major infectious diseases (e.g., tuberculosis, malaria, pneumonia, influenza, cholera, typhoid, smallpox, measles) from League of Nations and WHO statistical publications.
institutional_context: The setting is the international epidemiological transition beginning around 1940, when a cluster of global health innovations dramatically reduced mortality from major infectious diseases in poorer countries. Four developments drove this wave: mass production of penicillin and discovery of streptomycin and other antibiotics in the 1940s, which made bacterial killers like pneumonia and tuberculosis treatable; the discovery and widespread spraying of DDT against malaria-carrying mosquitoes; the founding of the World Health Organization (1948) and UNICEF, which diffused medicines, vaccines, and public health campaigns (including against smallpox and yellow fever) to less-developed regions; and a shift in international values toward universal health provision. Because countries differed sharply in their pre-1940 disease burdens—malaria endemic in South Asia and Central America but rare in Western Europe and the Southern Cone—these uniform global interventions affected life expectancy very unequally across countries, generating a sharp convergence in life expectancy between initially poor, middle-income, and rich nations.
